Fit a Bayesian false-positive occupancy model

Source: R/fp_occu.R
fp_occu.Rd

Fits the multiple-methods false-positive occupancy model of Miller et al. (2011) in Stan. Detections from an automated method may be false positives, whereas detections from a verified subset are certain. The occupancy probability depends on site covariates, true detection on observation (or site) covariates and an optional recorder random intercept, and the false-positive rate is either constant or a function of site covariates.

Usage

fp_occu(
  data,
  occ = ~1,
  det = ~1,
  fp = ~1,
  random_recorder = !is.null(data$recorder),
  ver = ~1,
  markov = NULL,
  random_fp = FALSE,
  random_det = FALSE,
  priors = fp_priors(),
  chains = 4,
  parallel_chains = chains,
  threads_per_chain = "auto",
  iter_warmup = 1000,
  iter_sampling = 1000,
  adapt_delta = 0.95,
  seed = NULL,
  refresh = NULL,
  ...
)

Arguments

data

An fp_data object from fp_data(), fp_data_wide(), or simulate_fp().

occ

One-sided formula for the logit of occupancy, using columns of data$sites.

det

One-sided formula for the logit of the true-detection probability of the automated method. It may use columns of data$auto and of data$sites. It must keep the intercept.

fp

One-sided formula for the logit of the false-positive rate, using columns of data$sites or, for covariates measured on each occasion (background noise, for instance), of data$auto; the rate then varies among the occasions of a site. ~ 1 (the default) fits a constant rate; ~ w lets the rate change along w. Use NULL to fit a standard occupancy model without false positives. The intercept is fixed by the model (see Details) and cannot be removed.

random_recorder

Logical. Add a recorder random intercept to true detection? Defaults to TRUE when data has a recorder column. Data from simulate_fp() always have one; with its default sd_recorder = 0 set this to FALSE, because a random effect whose true variance is zero causes divergent transitions.

ver

One-sided formula for the logit of the detection probability of the verified method, using columns of data$verified or data$sites (for example, who listened, or the length of the clip). The default, ~ 1, keeps it constant.

markov

Optional name of a numeric, date, or date-time column of data$auto that places the occasions of each site in time (an occasion number or a recording time). With it, true detection depends on whether the previous occasion of the same site was a detection, through the covariate y_prev added to det (reported as det_y_prev): a first-order Markov term for runs of detections, such as a bird calling for several consecutive minutes. See Details.

random_fp

Logical. Add a site random intercept to the logit of the false-positive rate, for rates that vary among sites in ways the covariates in fp do not capture. FALSE by default; see the section "Site random effect on the false-positive rate" before turning it on.

random_det

Logical. Add a site random intercept to the logit of the true-detection probability of the automated method, for detection that varies among occupied sites in ways the covariates in det do not capture (distance to the recorder, abundance, local noise). FALSE by default; it can be combined with random_fp. See the section "Site random effect on true detection".

priors

Prior settings from fp_priors().

chains, iter_warmup, iter_sampling, adapt_delta, seed

Passed to the $sample() method of 'cmdstanr'.

parallel_chains

Number of chains run in parallel.

threads_per_chain

Number of threads each chain uses to compute the likelihood, which is summed over sites in parallel with Stan's reduce_sum(). One of:

  • "auto": the physical cores divided among the parallel chains of this fit (not among other processes, such as calibration workers). The fastest choice for most data, but a fit is not reproduced exactly by its seed: with more than one thread the partial sums are added in an order that varies from run to run, so the draws drift apart after a while. The posterior is the same.

  • 1: each chain runs on one core, and the same seed gives the same draws. Use it when exact reproduction matters (published analyses, tests, saved results).

  • a larger number: that many threads per chain, with the same caveat as "auto". Keep parallel_chains * threads_per_chain at or below the number of cores.

Threads speed up fits with many sites or occasions (on the curiango data, 4 threads made each chain 3.4 times faster). The default is "auto" since crywolf 2.0.0 (it was 1 before). Under R CMD check (when _R_CHECK_LIMIT_CORES_ is set, as on CRAN) a fit uses at most two cores, counting parallel_chains * threads_per_chain.

refresh

How often each chain reports its progress, in iterations. The default, NULL, reports every 10% of the iterations in interactive sessions and nothing otherwise; 0 silences it. Warm-up iterations are usually slower than sampling ones, so the first half of the run takes more than half of the time.

...

Further arguments passed to $sample().

Value

An object of class fp_occu, with methods for base::print(), base::summary(), stats::coef(), stats::predict(), loo::loo(), and posterior::as_draws_df(). The 'cmdstanr' fit is in element fit.

Details

Identifiability. The intercept of the false-positive rate equals the intercept of true detection minus a positive gap, \(\gamma_0 = \alpha_1 - \Delta\), so that at the reference values of the covariates (all zero) a true detection is more likely than a false positive. This removes the label switching between the occupied and unoccupied states. Centre the covariates, so that the reference is an average site; simulate_fp() already returns them standardized.

Verified data. The verified detections anchor the false-positive rate. With none, the model still runs, but the rate is informed only by the priors and the gap, and the fit should not be trusted.

Observation-confirmation design. When data has confirmed occasions (argument confirmed of fp_data()), the model follows the observation-confirmation design of Chambert et al. (2015): an expert checks every observation of some automated occasions and finds only false ones, only true ones, both, or none. False observations can then occur at occupied sites too, and det and fp model \(s_1\) and \(s_0\), the probabilities of at least one true and at least one false observation on an occasion; a site-level detection at an occupied site has probability \(p_{11} = 1 - (1 - s_1)(1 - s_0)\), and p11_ref reports it at the reference. The confirmed occasions identify \(s_0\) directly, so verified data are optional; they can be combined with this design. The gap still applies, so that \(s_1 > s_0\) at the reference.

Site random effect on the false-positive rate. With random_fp = TRUE the logit of the false-positive rate of site \(i\) gains a term \(e_i \sim \mathrm{Normal}(0, \sigma_{fp})\), reported as sd_fp_site, with a half-Normal prior (fp_priors(fp_site_sd = )). In simulations with 300 sites, 20 automated occasions, and 30% of sites verified, it restored the coverage of the mean false-positive rate (p10_bar) when the rate varied among sites at random (from 0.00 and 0.55 with a constant rate to 0.95) and cost nothing when the rate was homogeneous. Use it with care:

  • It adds one parameter per site, and fits took 6 to 9 times longer.

  • It mixes less well: in those simulations the largest R-hat exceeded 1.01 in a quarter to three quarters of the fits. Check the diagnostics, and run longer chains (iter_warmup, iter_sampling) when they are poor.

  • Each site has a single latent state, so a site effect on false positives is told apart from occupancy mainly by the verified data; with few occasions or little verification it may be weakly identified.

  • It does not fix false positives that follow an environmental gradient. Those bias the occupancy effects, and the remedy is to put the occupancy covariates, and any measured correlate of the confusion, in fp (see below). Prefer covariates, and add the random effect for the variation that remains.

Predictions with predict(process = "fp") are for a site with \(e_i = 0\), a typical site.

Site random effect on true detection. With random_det = TRUE the logit of the true-detection probability of the automated method at site \(i\) gains a term \(d_i \sim \mathrm{Normal}(0, \sigma_{det})\), reported as sd_det_site, with a half-Normal prior (fp_priors(det_site_sd = )). It is for detection that varies among occupied sites for reasons the covariates in det do not capture, such as the distance from the recorder to the calling animals, their abundance, or local noise. The detection probability of the verified method has no site effect. p11_ref is the true-detection probability of a typical site (\(d_i = 0\)).

The two site effects answer different questions, and one cannot stand in for the other: in simulations where only detection varied among sites, a model with random_fp = TRUE alone attributed that variation to false positives and estimated a large sd_fp_site although the true rate was constant. Both can be fitted together. They are then identified by different data (true detection only at occupied sites, false positives only at unoccupied ones, with the verified data telling the two apart), but they mix slowly, and fp_occu() warns about it: check R-hat and the effective sample sizes, and run longer chains when they are poor. vignette("site_effects") shows both effects in simulations and on the curiango data.

Detections that come in runs. Occasions close in time are not independent when the species, once present, is active for a while: a calling bird is recorded in consecutive minutes, which makes detections more clustered among sites than independent occasions allow (a posterior predictive check flags it). markov adds the detection on the previous occasion as a covariate of true detection, so that \(p_{11}\) can be higher right after a detection. It acts on the occupied state only: false positives stay independent among occasions. y_prev is the detection on the occasion one time step earlier, where the step is the shortest interval between consecutive occasions of a site in the data (one occasion, or 15 minutes for recordings every 15 minutes). The first occasion of each site, and an occasion that follows a gap (for instance, a missing occasion), has y_prev = 0: its probability of detection is the one after no detection, so a run is not carried across a gap. Two occasions of a site at the same time are an error. fp_ppc() checks one step ahead, replicating each occasion given the observed previous one; simulate.fp_occu() simulates the runs sequentially.

When to model the false-positive rate. In the simulations behind this package, a constant rate gave calibrated intervals for the occupancy slope when false positives were homogeneous; random variation of the rate among sites made the estimate of the rate unreliable but largely spared the slope. When the rate tracked an environmental gradient correlated with the occupancy covariate and the confusion was strong, the slope was biased and verifying more sites did not fix it. Placing the occupancy covariate in fp recovered part of the calibration, and placing the gradient itself recovered all of it. Use fp_calibrate() to check your own design.

Parameter names. Coefficients are labelled by process and column of the design matrix: occ_* (occupancy), det_* (true detection), fp_* (false positive, where fp_(Intercept) is \(\gamma_0\)), plus fp_gap (\(\Delta\)), sd_recorder, p_verified (detection probability of the verified method), p11_ref and p10_ref (true- and false-positive probabilities at the reference), and p10_bar (false-positive probability averaged over sites or automated occasions, depending on the FP covariates). See crywolf-output for all names, scales, and availability conditions.

References

Chambert, T., Miller, D. A. W., & Nichols, J. D. (2015). Modeling false positive detections in species occurrence data under different study designs. Ecology, 96, 332–339. doi:10.1890/14-1507.1

Miller, D. A., Nichols, J. D., McClintock, B. T., Grant, E. H. C., Bailey, L. L., & Weir, L. A. (2011). Improving occupancy estimation when two types of observational error occur: non-detection and species misidentification. Ecology, 92, 1422–1428. doi:10.1890/10-1396.1

See also

crywolf-output, fp_data(), fp_priors(), fp_calibrate()

Examples

if (FALSE) { # \dontrun{
sim <- simulate_fp(nsite = 300, nocc = 20, conf_effect = 1.5,
                   conf_cor = 0.7, seed = 42)

# constant false-positive rate (the simulated recorders have no effect,
# so the recorder term is left out)
m0 <- fp_occu(sim$data, occ = ~ x, fp = ~ 1, random_recorder = FALSE)
# false-positive rate that tracks the occupancy covariate
m1 <- fp_occu(sim$data, occ = ~ x, fp = ~ x, random_recorder = FALSE)

coef(m0)["occ_x"]; coef(m1)["occ_x"]   # truth: -0.8
loo::loo_compare(loo(m0), loo(m1))
} # }
